evidence_note: JCO Global Oncology survey (data early 2020): average patient price of a 20-fraction course of external-beam radiotherapy on PPP-funded machines, in naira (US$1,810.67 at N357.14/$). "The average cost of a 20-fraction course of EBRT from PPP RT equipment was $1810.67 ± $598.13 (P$4,785.16 ± $1,580.73, ₦646,666.67 ± ₦213,619.60)"

Same survey: average patient price of a 20-fraction external-beam course on government-funded machines, in naira (US$416.50). PPP prices were about 335% higher. "which represents a 335% increase when compared with EBRT from government-funded RT at an average cost of $416.50 ± $153.52 (P$1,100.71 ± $405.72, ₦148,750 ± ₦54,829.28)."

Same survey: the share of the year that public external-beam machines were down, and its effect on throughput. PPP machines had no breakdown periods. "The government acquired and maintained EBRT equipment were nonfunctional 35% of the year (4.25 months ± 2.48 months), resulting in 60% fewer patients treated per year than PPP sponsored equipment"

NHIA Director-General (World Cancer Day 2025): federal health-insurance cost-sharing subsidy for radiotherapy, 50% of the bill capped at N400,000 per eligible patient. "To address this, the NHIA is now offering a 50 per cent subsidy on radiotherapy expenses, capped at N400,000."

Federal government via BusinessDay: patients supported by the Cancer Health Fund (CHF) over about three years, for about N2 billion in total. The article's per-patient cap is printed as '£2 million', probably a typo for naira; not verified. "So far, we have disbursed about N2 billion, benefiting 1,616 people over the past three years,"

Secondary news feature (Modern Ghana, Nov 2026): approximate price of a full radical breast radiotherapy course at National Hospital Abuja compared with other centres; primary source not named. "Full course radical breast cancer radiotherapy at National Hospital Abuja costs approximately ₦800,000, compared with about ₦1.2 million at some centres and more than ₦3 million at others."

Same publisher's Rivers State feature (Nov 2026): private-market price range for a six-week radiotherapy course (N1.2m to N1.8m), compared with the N400,000 NHIA cap. "At private market rates of N1.2 million to N1.8 million per six-week course, N400,000 covers only 22 to 33 percent"

The Guardian (World Cancer Day 2023), quoting medical experts: approximate price per radiotherapy treatment cycle, in naira. "radiotherapy costs about N1 million per treatment cycle while the average cost of treating cancer comprehensively for an individual is estimated at N20 million."

ARCON Secretary General (2022): price range for comprehensive cancer treatment (N500,000 to N1.5m), paid out of pocket and not covered by insurance. "a comprehensive cancer treatment costs between N500, 000.00 to N1.5 million and health insurance is still not covering cancer treatment."

One patient's quote reported by Nairametrics (Dec 2024): price of ten radiation sessions (N1.6m to N2m). This is a single patient's account, not a price list. "We've been informed that I will need to undergo ten radiation sessions, which will cost between N1.6 million and N2 million."

Pan African Medical Journal study at a public tertiary hospital in Ile-Ife: mean out-of-pocket cost of radiotherapy for breast cancer patients, in US$ (naira converted at N305.95/$, 2019). "The mean cost of radiotherapy was $462 (SD $223)"

BusinessDay (2019): typical purchase price range of a radiotherapy machine (US$1.5m to US$2m). "Findings by BusinessDay show that the average cost of a radiotherapy machine is between $1.5 million and $2 million, depending on the size and capacity."

Chief Clinical Oncologist at NSIA-LUTH (Prof. Francis Durosinmi-Etti), quoted in a secondary news feature as accurate for 2024: radiotherapy machine price with accessories (US$2m to US$4m). "price of radiotherapy machine ranges from $2m to $4m with all accessories."

BusinessDay (2019): value in US$ of the equipment and renovation that NSIA funded at the LUTH oncology department (the PPP centre). "the Oncology department at Lagos University Teaching Hospital (LUTH) Idi- Araba has received $11million (N3.96 billion) worth of sophisticated equipment and renovation from NSIA"

Annals of Medicine and Surgery editorial (2025): approximate capital cost in US$ of a basic radiotherapy centre (two teletherapy units, HDR brachytherapy, planning system, simulator, QA). Recurring costs are put at 5.5% to 15% of the investment, and yearly maintenance at US$41,390 for a linac against US$5,790 for cobalt. "costing around US$3 million. Recurring costs, including maintenance and source replacement, range from 5.5 to 15% of the initial investment."

IAEA guidance (Setting Up a Radiotherapy Programme, 2008): yearly long-term service contract as a share of purchase price, up to 15% for a linac and up to 8% for cobalt-60. "The annual cost of a long term service contract (without `glassware') may be up to 15% of the purchase price for a linac, and up to 8% for a 60Co unit."

Secondary news feature (Modern Ghana, Nov 2026): a corporate grant in US$ to repair National Hospital Abuja's linear accelerator after its machines went down (October 2026). "National Hospital Abuja publicly thanked Renaissance Africa Energy Company Limited for $300,000 to fix its Linear Accelerator."

IAEA guidance (2008): reference workload for a basic centre, about 500 new teletherapy patients a year (plus about 200 brachytherapy), run on two shifts. "a basic cancer therapy centre that treats approximately 500 new patients per year with teletherapy (about 50% of them with curative intent), and about 200 patients per year with brachytherapy. The work is organized into two shifts."

IAEA authors (Lancet Oncology 2021): planning assumption for megavoltage machine throughput, in patients per machine per year on an 8-hour day. "we assumed a machine throughput of 500 patients per year and a standard 8 h working day"

IAEA guidance (2008), Table 1: minimum staff for a basic radiotherapy clinic of about 500 teletherapy patients a year. "Four or five radiation oncologists Three or four medical physics staff Seven RTTs Three oncology nurses One maintenance technician/engineer"

IAEA guidance (2008), Table 5: staffing ratios that scale with patient load (radiation oncologists and physicists). "Staff radiation oncologist One additional for each 200-250 patients treated annually." ... "Radiation physicist One per centre for up to 400 patients annually. Additional in ratio of 1 per 400 patients treated annually."

National Hospital Abuja authors (JCO Global Oncology, 2020): daily linac throughput after adding a backup generator and newer machines (80 to 100 patients a day). "NHA also acquired a standby generator to ensure a steady power supply if the electrical grid failed. These improvements have reduced machine downtime and patient waiting times, allowing NHA to increase its radiation treatment capacity to 80 to 100 patients daily."

National Hospital Abuja's chief medical director (2019): patients and radiotherapy sessions (fractions) delivered on one linac since December 2017; 850 patients over 25,000+ sessions. "treated 850 patients in over 25,000 cycles of radiotherapy sessions"

LUTH Head of Oncology on the NSIA-funded centre (2019): expected monthly completed courses and daily patients, with a course taking about a month. "the facility will be able to treat at least more than 500 patients in a month with a complete session, but in a daily treatment we could have about 300 patients who can undergo treatment but not a complete session because it takes about a month to complete a session of treatment"

2025 IARC assessment as quoted by BusinessDay: named systems barriers to keeping radiotherapy running, namely the electricity supply and missing maintenance contracts outside PPPs. "Key challenges to continuous availability of radiotherapy services include disruptions in electricity supply and lack of maintenance contracts particularly in facilities outside the public-private partnerships framework,"

UCH Ibadan patient survey (January 2016): share of patients who had finished radiotherapy and still faced delays or cancellations (91.3%). "91.3% had experienced treatment delay or often cancellation due to healthcare worker strike, power failure, machine breakdown, or prolonged wait time."

Same UCH Ibadan survey: patients who could not pay for radiotherapy without help (80%), and the share with federal insurance (6%), which did not cover radiotherapy. "Eighty percent of patients could not afford radiotherapy without financial assistance and only 6% of the patients had federal insurance, which did not cover radiotherapy services."

JCO Global Oncology PPP survey (2021): describes how radiotherapy is paid for in Nigeria; no national out-of-pocket percentage is given for cancer care specifically. "Beyond the National Health Insurance Scheme for federal employees, which only covers about 5% of the population, the majority of patients pay out of pocket for treatment and a minority have private health insurance."
